paragraphs: Approximating a function involves deciding both how to predict its values and where to request additional observations. This paper introduces Active Nearest Neighbor Regressor, or ANNR, which combines nearest neighbor prediction with a geometric strategy for choosing new query points. It divides the input space into regions, each assigned a constant estimated function value.

The method uses the Voronoi-Delaunay framework to organize those regions and refine the approximation. Its query choices account for the geometry of the function’s graph. This provides an alternative to DEFER, the paper’s main comparison method, which progressively partitions the space into rectangles. ANNR addresses limitations arising from that rectangular subdivision strategy.

The authors provide an efficient implementation and theoretical guarantees that the algorithm halts. Their experiments report better performance than DEFER on explicitly defined mathematical functions and practical examples involving gravitational wave parameter inference and exploration of a generative model’s latent space. These findings support geometry-aware query selection as a useful approach to active function approximation.
icml-2022-active-nearest-neighbor-regres.tldr: ANNR uses geometric space refinement to choose function queries and improves on a rectangular-partitioning baseline in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction with advice from multiple experts when the learner can request only a small number of correct labels. The objective remains to keep regret low: the learner wants its accumulated performance to stay close to that of the best expert. The setting also permits a brief initial phase that can skip ahead to particularly informative examples.

The proposed algorithm uses Hedge, also called Exponential Weights, as a component. Its strong regret and label-efficiency guarantees depend on a particular structural property of the matrix containing the experts’ predictions. The authors call this property zeta-compactness. It describes a combinatorial condition under which selective label requests can support effective competition with the experts.

Compactness plays a role analogous to the disagreement coefficient used in active learning with independent, identically distributed data, but here the property is non-stochastic. The authors also provide a polynomial-time method that approximates compactness within a factor of three. Thus, the work supplies both a conditional learning guarantee and a way to assess its central structural quantity.
icml-2022-activehedge-hedge-meets-active.tldr: ActiveHedge achieves strong regret guarantees with few label requests under a specific combinatorial condition on expert predictions.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis allows later questions to depend on what earlier analyses revealed. Much of its theoretical foundation assumes that observations in the dataset are independent. This paper examines what remains possible when observations are correlated, making dependence within the sample a central part of the analysis.

The authors show that differential privacy can still guarantee generalization in some dependent-data settings. They quantify dependence through a notion called Gibbs-dependence. This makes the positive result explicitly sensitive to the relationships among observations, rather than treating privacy as an unconditional route to generalization. A tight negative example accompanies the guarantee and helps delineate the reach of the result.

The paper also extends the connection between transcript compression and adaptive analysis beyond independent, identically distributed observations. Here, the transcript represents the record of an adaptive interaction with the data. Together, the results show that two established approaches can remain useful with correlated observations, while demonstrating why dependence must be accounted for when stating their guarantees.
icml-2022-adaptive-data-analysis-with-co.tldr: The paper extends privacy and transcript-compression approaches to adaptive analysis with correlated data, with guarantees that account for dependence.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to preserve useful task knowledge while adapting to a different data domain. Conventional methods often access labeled source data and unlabeled target data together. This paper addresses the source-free setting, where that simultaneous access is unavailable. The challenge is to improve transfer without losing the distinctions needed to perform the task.

The authors analyze a tension in mapping original samples into a more generic domain: the mapping can improve transferability while weakening task discriminability. Their proposed response is mixup between an original sample and its corresponding translated generic sample. Theoretical and empirical analyses support this mixing strategy as a way to improve the balance between the two objectives.

The approach is implemented on top of existing source-free adaptation methods while respecting the setting’s restriction on source access. The authors report leading performance and faster convergence, with results extending beyond single-source adaptation. They also report improvements over earlier multi-source methods on classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, supporting the usefulness of the proposed trade-off across these tasks.
icml-2022-balancing-discriminability-and.tldr: Mixing original samples with their generic-domain translations improves the reported balance between task discrimination and source-free transfer.

paragraphs: This paper develops a batch version of Greenkhorn for entropically regularized optimal transport involving multiple marginal distributions. The framework includes several existing methods as special cases: Sinkhorn and Greenkhorn for two marginals, and greedy MultiSinkhorn for the general setting. This provides a common basis for studying algorithms that otherwise appear as separate procedures.

The convergence analysis uses iterative Bregman projections with greedy control. The authors establish a linear convergence rate, describing geometric progress toward the solution, and explicit bounds on the number of iterations required. When applied to the included algorithms, the analysis yields either new convergence rates or substantial improvements to previously available rates.

Batching also gives the method a practical degree of flexibility. Numerical experiments show that this flexibility can improve Sinkhorn’s performance in both two-marginal and multimarginal problems. The contribution therefore combines a unified theoretical treatment with evidence that choices about how updates are grouped can matter computationally, alongside the guarantees governing convergence.
icml-2022-batch-greenkhorn-algorithm-for.tldr: A batch Greenkhorn framework unifies transport algorithms, strengthens convergence guarantees, and offers empirical performance gains through flexible batching.

paragraphs: Probabilistic predictions should be informative and reliable about their uncertainty. Calibration concerns whether the probabilities a model reports agree with observed outcomes; sharpness concerns how concentrated its predictions are. This paper addresses the fact that standard maximum-likelihood training can produce poorly calibrated models, so a stated confidence level may not match its actual frequency of success.

The authors introduce a training procedure based on recalibration through low-dimensional density estimation. It targets distribution calibration, a general calibration property, and applies to arbitrary models, including neural networks. The approach is intended to improve the reliability of the predictive distribution while preserving overall predictive performance.

The theoretical correctness result assumes that the required low-dimensional densities can be estimated. The paper also establishes uniform convergence bounds and reports empirical improvements for linear and deep Bayesian models. These results connect a practical recalibration procedure to a precise statistical condition: the calibration guarantee rests on density estimation, while the experiments show benefits in the evaluated model families.
icml-2022-calibrated-and-sharp-uncertain.tldr: Low-dimensional density estimation supports a broadly applicable recalibration procedure with conditional theoretical guarantees and reported predictive improvements.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing seeks provable robustness by introducing randomness around a classifier’s input. Existing certification approaches based on likelihood ratios cannot handle certain noise distributions whose possible values lie within a bounded set. Uniform distributions over bounded regions are an important example addressed by this paper.

The authors generalize a framework based on f-divergence into frameworks using Wasserstein distance and total variation distance. This change enables theoretical and experimental analysis of smoothing distributions with bounded support. They apply the methodology to uniform distributions over balls defined by several lp norms, including the one, two, and infinity norms and a general case.

For perturbations measured with l1, l2, and linfinity norms, the paper proves negative certified-robustness properties for the cases studied. These results characterize constraints on certification rather than promising that every newly analyzable distribution gives strong protection. Experiments using ResNet on CIFAR-10 validate the theory, and the authors state that their certification procedure has constant computation time. The contribution expands the scope of analysis while exposing unfavorable robustness properties.
icml-2022-certified-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Distance-based certification frameworks analyze bounded-support smoothing and establish negative robustness properties for the uniform distributions studied.

paragraphs: Prompt-based learning can work with few or no labeled examples, but it can be brittle and require large models. This paper investigates whether unlabeled data can improve that situation through co-training. The proposed process improves the original prompt model while also learning a smaller model specialized for the downstream task.

The adaptation mechanism depends on the access available to the prompt model. When only outputs such as GPT-3 probabilities are accessible, the authors learn a calibration model over those outputs. When gradients are accessible but full fine-tuning is too costly, as in their T0 setting, they instead learn continuous soft-prompt vectors that iteratively update the prompt model’s behavior.

The authors report significant improvements on challenging datasets where prompting initially trails fully supervised learning by a large margin. The findings show how co-training can use unlabeled data under two distinct access constraints. They also give the process two useful outcomes: a stronger prompting system and a smaller task-specific model learned alongside it.
icml-2022-co-training-improves-prompt-ba.tldr: Co-training with unlabeled data improves prompt-based models while training smaller task-specific models under different levels of model access.

paragraphs: Pretrained generative models have broad capabilities, but their outputs may violate requirements of a particular task. Examples include hallucinations in summaries and style violations in generated code. Adapting a model to such requirements creates another concern: the adaptation may damage its existing capabilities, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting.

Earlier work represents task requirements with energy-based models and approximates the resulting distributions using distributional policy gradients. That approach was limited to unconditional generation. This paper introduces Conditional DPG, or CDPG, extending the method to tasks where generation depends on an input, such as translating a supplied passage or summarizing a document.

The authors evaluate four control objectives across translation, summarization, and code generation, using T5 and GPT-Neo. In these experiments, CDPG consistently moves the pretrained models closer to the control objectives without the catastrophic forgetting observed with comparison approaches. The result supports conditional distributional adaptation as a way to improve task-specific behavior while retaining general capabilities in the tested settings.
icml-2022-controlling-conditional-langua.tldr: CDPG extends distributional policy gradients to conditional generation, improving tested control objectives without observed catastrophic forgetting.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiple agents learning simultaneously in a Markov decision process and sharing information to reduce their individual regret. The setting covers both stochastic and adversarial environments. A central question is how the benefit of cooperation changes depending on the way randomness is shared across agents.

With fresh randomness, each agent receives an independently sampled trajectory. With non-fresh randomness, the episode’s costs and transitions are fixed in a shared realization before interaction begins. Consequently, agents taking the same action in the same state at the same time observe the same cost and next state. Their own actions still influence which trajectories they experience.

The authors analyze the relevant combinations of these settings and prove upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match. The distinction matters because collecting experiences from several agents need not produce independent observations. By explicitly modeling this difference, the paper characterizes the challenges and attainable performance of cooperation, including non-fresh randomness and adversarial MDPs as new settings in its stated research context.
icml-2022-cooperative-online-learning-in.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching regret bounds for cooperative learning under independent or shared randomness in stochastic and adversarial MDPs.

paragraphs: Sharing information across users can reduce the interactions needed to learn a recommendation policy. This paper asks what happens when an unknown fraction alpha, smaller than one half, consists of arbitrary adversarial users. The remaining users share the same contextual bandit problem, and the goal is to learn a policy that performs well for them.

The authors prove that adversarial users fundamentally weaken the gains from collaboration. Unless the number of users is super-polynomial, their lower bound on per-user interactions grows with the smaller of the numbers of contexts and actions, multiplied by alpha squared and inverse accuracy squared, up to logarithmic factors. This differs from the stated non-adversarial requirement, which depends only on inverse accuracy squared.

The proposed defense uses efficient robust mean estimators for scalar and high-dimensional observations. Its upper bound has a similar form but depends on alpha rather than alpha squared, leaving a gap between the bounds. The authors also show that context distributions can permit improvements, making the achievable protection sensitive to the problem’s structure.
icml-2022-coordinated-attacks-against-co.tldr: Adversarial users reduce contextual-bandit collaboration gains, and robust mean estimation provides defenses with explicit interaction bounds.

paragraphs: Traffic flow depends on interactions across a road network and on how those interactions evolve over time. This makes forecasting difficult for models that rely on a predefined, static graph. DSTAGNN addresses the problem by using historical traffic observations to construct a graph that reflects dynamic spatial and temporal information.

The network combines two mechanisms for representing these dependencies. An improved multi-head attention mechanism represents changing spatial relevance among road-network nodes. Multi-scale gated convolution captures temporal relationships through features with different receptive fields, allowing the architecture to draw on patterns spanning different temporal ranges. The graph construction and network architecture together target the evolving relationships present in traffic data.

Experiments on real-world datasets report significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings support the paper’s premise that historical observations contain useful information about the network’s dynamic structure. The contribution is both a data-driven replacement for the static graph and an architecture designed to use spatial relevance alongside temporal patterns at multiple scales.
icml-2022-dstagnn-dynamic-spatial-tempor.tldr: DSTAGNN combines a data-driven dynamic graph, attention, and multi-scale temporal convolution to improve reported traffic forecasts.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from too few linear measurements to determine it uniquely without additional knowledge. A prior supplies information about the kinds of signals that are plausible. This paper addresses an added difficulty: the signal may have an unknown orientation before the measurements are taken, so recovery must accommodate that uncertainty.

The authors propose equivariant generative models as priors, with orientation information represented in their latent space. They construct an equivariant variational autoencoder and use its decoder to generate candidate signals. Reconstruction then proceeds through iterative gradient descent in the model’s latent space, searching for a representation that recovers the signal despite its unknown orientation.

The paper shows recovery with this approach and provides additional theoretical guarantees. Its central contribution is to make orientation part of the generative representation used for reconstruction. The authors also discuss possible improvements in convergence and latency. Those computational benefits are presented as potential gains, while latent-space recovery and the accompanying guarantees form the stated core results.
icml-2022-equivariant-priors-for-compres.tldr: Equivariant generative priors enable latent-space reconstruction of compressed signals with unknown orientation, supported by theoretical recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an underlying ordering of candidates from voters’ preferences. It assumes the preferences are single-peaked along an axis: each voter has a preferred point, with less preferred candidates farther away along either side. The learning problem is to identify that axis by sampling votes.

For several natural distributions of preferences, the authors establish tight bounds on the required number of samples. A striking feature is that these bounds do not depend on the number of candidates. Under the distributions studied, adding candidates therefore does not force the number of sampled votes to grow. The distributional qualification is central to the scope of this result.

The analysis also considers preferences generated from two axes over the same candidates, including cases where one axis is known. Finally, the authors study learning from pairwise comparisons and from equivalence queries rather than only complete votes. These extensions examine how recovering preference structure changes when the population’s structure or the available form of feedback changes.
icml-2022-exact-learning-of-preference-s.tldr: For several preference distributions, the axis underlying single-peaked votes can be learned with sample bounds independent of candidate count.

paragraphs: FedScale is a benchmarking suite designed to make federated learning research more realistic and reproducible. It brings together datasets and a runtime so researchers can evaluate both model behavior and system performance. The covered tasks include image classification, object detection, language modeling, and speech recognition, giving the suite a broad range of learning workloads.

Each dataset includes a unified evaluation protocol with real-world data splits and evaluation metrics. The runtime is designed to scale and to support extensions. Its high-level interfaces help researchers implement federated algorithms, deploy them across different hardware and software backends, and evaluate them at scale with relatively little development effort.

The authors use the datasets and runtime together for systematic benchmarking. Their experiments highlight opportunities to optimize learning and system behavior jointly while accounting for heterogeneity across the federated setting. FedScale’s contribution is therefore shared evaluation infrastructure as well as experimental evidence about useful optimization directions. The paper also presents the suite as open-source infrastructure for community participation.
icml-2022-fedscale-benchmarking-model-an.tldr: FedScale combines realistic datasets, standardized evaluation, and a scalable runtime for reproducible federated learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Many estimation problems in causal inference, economics, and robust machine learning can be expressed through conditional moment restrictions. These require certain average relationships to hold conditional on other information. Estimation is challenging because such requirements correspond to a continuum of unconditional restrictions, rather than a finite list that can be handled directly.

Previous approaches extend the generalized method of moments to this setting. The paper instead develops a functional version of generalized empirical likelihood, a broader framework with previously established favorable small-sample properties relative to GMM estimators. Its reformulation allows arbitrary models to be incorporated, creating a route for using modern machine learning within this estimation framework.

A dual formulation of the infinite-dimensional optimization problem motivates a practical estimation method. The authors investigate its asymptotic properties and implement it using both kernels and neural networks. These implementations achieve state-of-the-art empirical performance on two conditional moment restriction problems. The work thus connects a flexible statistical formulation to usable estimators and evidence of strong performance in the evaluated problems.
icml-2022-functional-generalized-empiric.tldr: A functional reformulation of generalized empirical likelihood enables kernel and neural estimators for conditional moment restrictions.

paragraphs: Functional output regression predicts an output that is itself a function. This paper examines how the choice of loss can make such regression more flexible in dealing with outliers and sparsity. Much of the existing work uses squared loss, while the authors develop alternatives based on extensions of Huber and epsilon-insensitive losses.

These losses are constructed through infimal convolution, which supplies the mathematical foundation for the proposed framework. The aim is to accommodate different forms of outliers and sparsity within functional output regression. This places the treatment of those properties inside the regression objective, making loss design a central part of how the prediction problem is formulated.

The authors derive computationally tractable algorithms using duality in vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. They demonstrate the approach’s efficiency on synthetic and real-world benchmarks and compare it with the conventional squared-loss formulation. The contribution joins a flexible family of objectives with algorithms for solving them, showing how alternatives to squared loss can be used in the functional-output setting.
icml-2022-functional-output-regression-w.tldr: The paper develops tractable functional-output regression methods using extended Huber and epsilon-insensitive losses to handle outliers and sparsity.

paragraphs: Adversarial generation is difficult for text because discrete outputs interrupt the usual gradient path from a discriminator back to a generator. Training the generator through reinforcement learning provides an alternative, but the discriminator’s changing rewards and vanishing gradients create further difficulties. Such methods can also underperform direct maximum-likelihood training.

The paper introduces Generative Cooperative Networks, which use the discriminator architecture cooperatively with the generation policy to produce realistic text for a task. This changes the role of the discriminator within generation. Its contribution is brought together with the policy in the sampling process, providing a different way to use the information the discriminator supplies.

The authors give theoretical convergence guarantees for their approach and investigate efficient decoding schemes. Their empirical study reports state-of-the-art performance on two natural-language-generation tasks. The work therefore combines a cooperative formulation with both theoretical analysis and practical decoding choices. The reported findings support this formulation as a productive approach to the optimization difficulties associated with discrete language generation.
icml-2022-generative-cooperative-network.tldr: Generative Cooperative Networks combine discriminator information with a generation policy, with convergence guarantees and strong reported text-generation results.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents often train on stored experiences, and the choice of which experiences to replay can affect learning speed. Existing non-uniform sampling methods have limited theoretical foundations. This paper treats replay-buffer sampling as an importance-sampling problem for gradient estimation, giving a principled objective for choosing a sampling distribution.

The authors derive the theoretically optimal distribution under this formulation, associated with the best theoretical convergence speed. They also use that analysis to provide new foundations for Prioritized Experience Replay. Because the optimal distribution is intractable, they develop practical approximations, including Large Batch Experience Replay, or LaBER, which they describe as efficient and easy to implement.

LaBER can be combined with Deep Q-Networks, distributional reinforcement learning, and actor-critic methods. Experiments across Atari games and PyBullet environments report improvements over the underlying agents and other prioritization schemes. The significance is the link between theory and implementation: an ideal gradient-sampling calculation guides approximate replay methods that show practical benefits in the evaluated environments.
icml-2022-large-batch-experience-replay-.tldr: LaBER approximates theoretically motivated replay sampling and improves reported reinforcement learning performance across Atari and PyBullet tasks.

paragraphs: Neural scene representations often use positional encoding to help a multilayer perceptron capture spatial detail. Choosing the encoding’s frequencies creates a trade-off: high frequencies can introduce noise in simple regions, while low frequencies can miss fine detail. This paper addresses scenes that contain both kinds of structure across a wide frequency range.

Progressive Implicit Networks expose a hierarchical network to progressively expanded sets of frequency encodings. The model learns multiple levels of scene detail without requiring explicit supervision for each level. Each level also defines its own continuous implicit representation, so a representation can be used separately at the resolution it supports.

This modularity means that a coarser reconstruction can use a smaller network. Experiments on several two-dimensional and three-dimensional datasets report improvements in reconstruction accuracy, representational capacity, and training speed relative to the baselines. The approach connects frequency selection with network hierarchy, allowing one learned model to represent scenes progressively while making its individual levels useful for different reconstruction resolutions.
icml-2022-pins-progressive-implicit-netw.tldr: PINs progressively introduce frequency encodings into a hierarchical network to learn modular scene representations at multiple levels of detail.

paragraphs: Probabilistic solvers for ordinary differential equations support uncertainty quantification and inference about dynamical systems. Scaling these methods to high-dimensional equations has been obstructed by matrix-matrix computations within every solver step. This paper explains the mathematical assumptions and implementation schemes that make much larger probabilistic numerical solutions possible.

The efficient formulations rely on one of two kinds of structure in the prior model: independence assumptions or Kronecker structure. These are substantive modeling ingredients behind the computational improvement. Organizing the prior in these ways enables the method to address the expensive operations that previously prevented high-dimensional use.

The authors evaluate efficiency on a range of problems, including a probabilistic simulation with millions of dimensions. Such scale matters particularly for partial differential equations that become large systems of ordinary differential equations after discretization. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a practical demonstration and an explanation of the structure supporting it, connecting high-dimensional computation with the assumptions used to represent numerical uncertainty.
icml-2022-probabilistic-ode-solutions-in.tldr: Independence assumptions or Kronecker-structured priors enable probabilistic ODE solvers to scale to demonstrated problems with millions of dimensions.

paragraphs: Scientific time series often provide different views of one underlying dynamical system. Neuroscience experiments, for example, may record electrophysiological and behavioral observations together. This paper develops an unsupervised framework that combines such modalities to reconstruct nonlinear dynamics and analyze relationships between the observed data domains.

The framework uses dynamically interpretable recurrent neural networks to represent the underlying system. Modality-specific decoders from the generalized linear model family connect that shared dynamics model to each type of observation. The authors develop and compare expectation-maximization and variational-inference algorithms for training, providing two ways to fit the combined model.

On nonlinear dynamical-system benchmarks, the methods use information from other channels to compensate efficiently when one channel is too noisy or has missing information. An application to experimental neuroscience data demonstrates how the algorithm links different observation domains to the underlying dynamics. These findings support integrating simultaneous measurements within a shared dynamical model, especially when the available channels provide uneven amounts of usable information.
icml-2022-reconstructing-nonlinear-dynam.tldr: A shared recurrent dynamics model with modality-specific decoders reconstructs nonlinear systems and uses complementary channels to compensate for noisy or missing observations.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning algorithms are trained from existing data, but comparing them can still involve online evaluations during model selection. This paper argues that the available evaluation budget is part of a meaningful comparison. Different problems permit different amounts of evaluation, and the preferred algorithm can change with that budget.

The authors demonstrate this budget dependence across robotics, finance, and energy management. They recommend reporting performance over varying online evaluation budgets. To support that reporting, they adopt Expected Validation Performance, a tool from natural language processing that estimates expected maximum performance at different budgets using results already produced by hyperparameter search.

The method requires no additional computation beyond that search. Applying it also reveals that Behavioral Cloning is often more favorable than offline reinforcement learning algorithms when the evaluation budget is limited. The finding does not establish a universally preferred method; it shows why the resources available for selecting a model can affect practical conclusions about algorithm quality and should be visible in reported comparisons.
icml-2022-showing-your-offline-reinforce.tldr: Offline reinforcement learning rankings can change with online evaluation budgets, making budget-aware performance reporting essential to the paper’s proposed comparisons.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but its performance can suffer when the unlabeled set’s class balance differs from what the algorithm expects. This paper addresses learning when that distribution is unknown. It focuses on weighting the consistency loss used by consistency-based semi-supervised methods.

The authors first investigate whether adding weights to this loss is feasible and examine the need for smoothing those weights. They then propose Smoothed Adaptive Weighting, or SAW. The algorithm estimates how difficult each class is to learn and uses those estimates to construct the weights, adapting the learning process to differences among classes.

SAW is designed to complement existing consistency-based algorithms without assuming a distribution for the unlabeled data. The authors report improved reliability on three standard datasets and a gigapixel medical imaging application. These findings support class-difficulty estimates and smoothed weighting as useful additions when class imbalance makes fixed expectations about unlabeled examples unreliable, with the demonstrated benefits spanning the evaluated benchmark and application settings.
icml-2022-smoothed-adaptive-weighting-fo.tldr: SAW adapts smoothed consistency-loss weights to estimated class difficulty, improving reported reliability without assuming the unlabeled class distribution.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can struggle to infer relationships and causal structure from experience. This paper investigates whether language can help them acquire that knowledge, as explanations help human learners. The approach augments an agent’s experience by training it to predict language descriptions and explanations alongside learning in complex environments.

The authors show that language supports learning on challenging relational tasks and investigate which aspects of language contribute to that benefit. They then extend the analysis to causal structure. Explanations can influence how agents generalize beyond training conditions when the original experience is ambiguous and contains causal confounding.

The experiments also show that explanations can help agents learn to perform interventions to identify causal relationships. This goes beyond recognizing a relationship in observed experience: the agent learns to take actions that help resolve causal questions. Together, the results suggest that language descriptions and explanations may improve learning and generalization by shaping the relational and causal knowledge agents acquire in the studied environments.
icml-2022-tell-me-why-explanations-suppo.tldr: Training agents to predict descriptions and explanations supports relational learning, causal generalization, and experimental interventions in the studied environments.
